SoyaSoybeansSoybeans Slip as Harvest Accelerates and US Exports Edge Ahead of BrazilCMBCMB News EditorialEditorial DeskOctober 19, 2026Soybean prices ease on faster US harvest and technical selling, while US export values undercut Brazil and funds trim longs. Concise outlook and trading tips.Soybean futures extended their recent decline, with the CBOT November contract sliding to its lowest close since late August as technical selling combined with improving US harvest weather. At the same time, US export offers have gained a clear price edge over Brazil, but Chinese demand remains restrained by a 10% import tariff despite sizable new USDA‑confirmed sales. Global oilseed markets remain mixed: soybeans and soy oil weakened, while palm oil futures in Malaysia rallied strongly on surging exports and robust Indian buying. In Europe, soybean production is slowly shifting northward, yet the EU still relies on imports for over 90% of its soybean consumption. Fund positioning shows a first notable reduction in net long exposure, suggesting waning speculative support while physical demand and weather remain in focus. Prices Chicago soybeans ended last week under pressure, with the November contract closing at its lowest level since August 25, reflecting both technical selling and harvest‑related hedging. The weakness in soybean oil in Chicago added to the negative tone across the soy complex, spilling over into canola at ICE Winnipeg and rapeseed at Euronext. In the physical market, indicative offers from the CMB platform show relatively stable to slightly firmer export values for selected origins. Soybeans FOB Washington D.C. (US, No. 2) are quoted at 0.58 EUR/kg (unchanged since October 2). Ukrainian soybeans FOB Odesa have edged up to 0.333 EUR/kg (from 0.327 EUR/kg on October 9), while GMO‑free soybeans CPT Odesa are at 0.401 EUR/kg (up from 0.396 EUR/kg on October 15). Indian soybeans (sortex clean) FOB New Delhi are stable at 0.89 EUR/kg, and Chinese yellow soybeans FOB Beijing hold at 0.74 EUR/kg, with organic yellow soybeans at 0.85 EUR/kg. On the international trade side, US soybeans currently enjoy a clear price advantage versus Brazilian origin. As of October 15, US soybeans for November shipment were quoted at 505.23 US‑dollars per tonne FOB New Orleans, compared with 517.38 US‑dollars per tonne FOB Santos for Brazilian beans. This discount is helping to redirect some demand toward the US despite ongoing tariff headwinds in China. Supply & Demand Fundamentally, the latest downward move is driven by improving supply expectations. Dry, more settled weather is forecast across much of the US Midwest this week, allowing soybean harvest to accelerate after earlier delays. Recent USDA Crop Progress updates confirm that harvest has been catching up in parts of the Corn Belt as conditions have turned drier, easing concerns about field losses and logistical bottlenecks. Export dynamics, however, remain nuanced. Despite a still‑dampening 10% Chinese import tariff on US soybeans, Beijing has returned to the US market on a notable scale. The USDA confirmed new sales of 558,000 tonnes of US soybeans to China on Friday alone, bringing total reported sales to China this week to 1.358 million tonnes. Additional weekly sales of 236,000 tonnes to unknown destinations—519,450 tonnes in total for the week—likely include further Chinese demand. Weekly export sales for the week ending October 8 reached 574,878 tonnes, 5% above the previous week but still 27% below the same week a year earlier. Europe remains structurally import dependent. While soybean acreage is gradually shifting northward into Poland, northern France and Germany, plantings in southern EU regions are shrinking due to worsening drought and irrigation difficulties. Overall EU soybean area is thus broadly stable according to Protealis, but more than 90% of EU soybean consumption still has to be covered by imports. This entrenched import dependency keeps European crushers and feed manufacturers sensitive to shifts in global supply, freight and currency conditions. The latest CFTC report for the week to October 13 shows investment funds cutting their net long position in soybeans by 14,169 contracts to 237,491 contracts. This trimming of length follows a period of elevated bullish positioning and reflects a more cautious stance as harvest pressure builds and chart support levels are tested. Product‑side demand signals are mixed. In the week to October 8, US export sales of soybean meal totaled 366,314 tonnes, squarely in the middle of market expectations, indicating steady but unspectacular demand from feed users. In contrast, export sales of soybean oil reached only 1,208 tonnes, underscoring the current softness in vegoil demand against a backdrop of uncertain biofuel policy and stiff competition from palm oil and sunflower oil. By contrast, the Malaysian palm oil market showed pronounced strength. The January contract on Bursa Malaysia surged by 44 ringgit on Friday to 4,769 ringgit per tonne—equivalent to roughly 3.9% gains on the week—driven by sharply higher exports in the first half of October (up 43–58% versus the same period in September) and a seven‑month high in Indian palm oil imports. This divergence—firmer palm oil versus weaker soy oil—narrows the relative discount of palm oil and may eventually lend some indirect support to the soy complex if substitution flows shift again. Weather & Regional Production Shifts Weather is currently a bearish short‑term factor for soybeans. Forecasts call for drier conditions across much of the US Midwest this week, improving field access and allowing combines to return to wetter areas, particularly in parts of Iowa and the eastern Corn Belt. As harvest accelerates, nearby basis levels and futures are likely to stay under pressure until clearer evidence emerges on final yields and farmer selling behavior. In Europe, climate trends are reshaping soybean geography. Northern regions such as Poland, northern France and Germany are expanding soybean area, benefiting from milder summers and improved varietal adaptation. In contrast, southern Europe is losing soybean acreage as chronic drought and water scarcity make irrigation more expensive and less reliable. While total EU output may remain broadly stable in the near term, the northward shift could, over time, alter quality profiles, logistics flows and crush economics within the bloc. Short-Term Outlook & Trading Ideas Near‑term sentiment in soybeans remains moderately bearish as harvest pressure, weaker soy oil prices and reduced speculative length outweigh the supportive signal from recent export sales to China. However, the emerging US price advantage over Brazil and strong palm oil pricing form a constructive medium‑term backdrop once the bulk of the US harvest is complete and on‑farm selling slows. Importers / Crushers: Use current futures weakness and still‑comfortable physical availability to extend nearby coverage, especially for Q4 2026–Q1 2027 needs. Consider scaling in purchases rather than waiting for an elusive further drop, given US FOB values already undercut Brazil. Producers (US/EU): Hedge a portion of unpriced production on rebounds toward recent resistance, while keeping some upside open via options in case of later South American weather issues or stronger Chinese demand. Speculators: Bias remains mildly short‑term bearish, but risk‑reward for fresh shorts is deteriorating as funds have already reduced length. Look for signs of capitulation selling or stronger basis before shifting back to a more neutral or cautiously long stance. 3-Day Directional View Market / Location Contract / Term Directional Bias (Next 3 Days) CBOT Soybeans Nearby futures Slightly bearish to sideways – harvest pressure and technical selling dominate, but export sales limit downside. SoyaSoybeansSoybeans Steady as Futures Firm but Physical Differentials DivergeCMBCMB News EditorialEditorial DeskOctober 19, 2026Concise soybean market update: CBOT futures and crush, China DCE moves, FOB basis levels in US, Ukraine, India and China, plus weather and 3‑day outlook.Soybean futures are edging higher on the CBOT and stabilising on China’s DCE, while physical FOB and CPT prices in key origins show a mixed but broadly steady picture. Crush margins remain supported by firmer soymeal and slightly softer soyoil, keeping demand for beans underpinned despite export competition and macro headwinds. The soybean complex is currently characterised by modest gains in CBOT beans and meal alongside marginal softness in soyoil, signalling a crush-friendly structure. China’s Dalian No. 1 soybeans are slightly lower on the week, but still at historically firm levels, while recent export data confirm China’s continued heavy reliance on South American origin and selective US purchases. In the physical market, FOB New Delhi and Beijing offers are firm, while Ukrainian FOB/CPT values have ticked higher from recent lows. Weather in the US Midwest is allowing harvest to progress, and early planting conditions in Brazil’s Mato Grosso are broadly adequate, limiting immediate supply concerns. Prices On the CBOT, nearby soybean futures are modestly higher: November 2026 trades at 1,264.00 US‑cent/bu (+0.22% versus the previous close), with January 2027 at 1,279.00 US‑cent/bu (+0.25%). Forward spreads remain only slightly carry, with May 2027 at 1,295.00 US‑cent/bu and July 2027 at 1,300.25 US‑cent/bu, reflecting comfortable but not burdensome projected supplies. Products point to supportive crush margins. December 2026 soymeal is at 358.80 USD/short ton (+0.48% on the day), with the 2027 curve only marginally lower, while December 2026 soyoil trades at 67.04 US‑cent/lb (‑0.13%) and holds a gentle downward tilt along the 2027 strip. This combination of firmer meal and slightly softer oil is typically constructive for crushers’ bean demand. In China, DCE No.1 soybeans for November 2026 settle at 5,378 CYN/t (‑0.30% day‑on‑day), with January 2027 at 5,422 CYN/t (‑0.31%). The curve remains narrowly backwardated around 5,4–5,6k CYN/t, signalling firm domestic values even after a small correction. In the US, harvest is progressing well; regional reports from the Midwest indicate that a run of dry weather in mid‑October allowed rapid soybean combining, despite corn lagging slightly behind average. The latest international market wire also highlights that soybean futures recently sold off before finding buying interest, with decent export sales and ongoing flash sales to China and unknown destinations underpinning demand. In Brazil, 2026/27 soybean planting is advancing quickly. Mato Grosso planting is reported at around 52% complete, ahead of its five‑year average near 43%, though some northern areas complain about dryness. Earlier seasonal outlooks linked to El Niño stress the importance of regular rainfall for yield potential, particularly in central and northern Brazil, but so far farmers have mostly stayed on schedule, limiting weather‑driven risk premia. On the demand side, China remains the pivotal buyer. Newly released customs‑based trade snapshots show non‑seed soybean imports in August 2026 at about USD 5.85 billion, up 7.5% year‑on‑year and confirming structurally strong dependence on foreign beans. At the same time, recent private‑sector reporting emphasises that Brazil continues to dominate China’s 2026 import program, with the US sharing a smaller slice of the pie despite periodic cargo purchases. Recent commentary notes that September US crush was the lowest in 13 months, reflecting some moderation in domestic processing demand, though meal exports and new US sales to China still help clear supply. Overall, the current balance suggests adequate global availabilities with firm but not explosive import demand. Brazil (Mato Grosso & central belt): Early‑season assessments described patchy soil moisture and the need for more regular rains from mid‑October; more recent field commentary suggests planting is nonetheless slightly ahead of average, with dryness complaints mainly in northern zones but no widespread stress yet. For now, weather is a background influence rather than a primary bullish driver, but traders will closely monitor rainfall distribution across central Brazil over the coming weeks as a key determinant of 2026/27 yield potential. Market implications & positioning The current futures structure, with nearby CBOT soybeans around 1,260–1,300 US‑cent/bu and a gently rising curve into 2028, suggests that the market is pricing in comfortable but not excessive stocks, and that large downward moves may require a clear deterioration in demand or a bearish supply shock. Meanwhile, strengthening FOB/CPT quotations from Ukraine and firm Indian and Chinese offers indicate a floor under physical prices, especially for GMO‑free and organic segments. Speculative positioning data in public commentary point to broader commodity index outflows, but soybeans are holding key chart support areas, with recent technical commentary noting that bean futures and other row crops have so far defended major moving averages. This argues for a more range‑bound environment in the near term, with weather headlines and Chinese buying pace acting as primary catalysts for any break‑out. Trading outlook Importers/feed buyers: Consider layering in Q4‑Q1 coverage on price dips near the lower end of the recent CBOT range, particularly for premium GMO‑free (Ukraine CPT) and organic (China FOB) beans, where local price trends are gently upwards. Producers (US, Brazil, Ukraine): Use modest futures rallies and firm local basis to extend incremental sales rather than wait for a major weather scare; the flat futures curve and solid South American production outlook currently cap upside. Traders/crushers: Crush margins look constructive with strong meal and slightly softer oil; maintaining long meal/short oil structures against delta‑hedged beans remains justified while this relationship holds. 3‑day directional outlook CBOT Soybeans (Nov/Jan): Slightly firmer bias, with good US harvest progress and steady Chinese demand likely keeping trade within a moderate range. DCE Soybeans No.1: Mostly sideways to marginally softer after recent small declines, but underpinned by robust import dependence and crush demand.
